title: Budget and kill rules
summary: Exact starting rules for when to kill, hold, keep or scale an ad set, how to scale a winner and when to stop a whole test. You set your numbers before launch, apply one rule card at fixed checkpoints and protect your bankroll with written loss caps.

lessons.title: Set your numbers before launch
objectives: By the end you can work out break-even CPA, target CPA and the scale line from one payout.
By the end you can set a zero-conversion kill line and a CPA kill line for any offer.
By the end you can size the test budget and daily budget for each ad set.

steps.p: Every kill, hold or scale decision compares a result with a line. If the line is not written before launch, you will draw it after you see the result, and you will draw it where it makes you feel better. That habit is how a planned $90 test turns into a $400 loss.

d.b: Draw the lines before you spend
d.s: Starting rules; adapt to your vertical and data.

steps.say: Here's the big idea of this whole module. Every kill, hold or scale decision compares a result with a line. If you don't write that line before launch, you'll draw it after you see the result, and you'll draw it wherever it makes you feel better. That's exactly how a planned ninety dollar test quietly turns into a four hundred dollar loss. So we draw the lines before we spend. And remember, these are starting rules. Adapt them to your vertical and your data.

steps.h: The six numbers on your plan
steps.p: Before any ad goes live you write six numbers on one page. All six come from the payout and the margin you want to keep. The rest of this module uses them at every checkpoint, so get them right once and you never have to argue with yourself later.
d: Payout|what the network pays per FTD or lead
Break-even CPA|the most you can pay without losing
Target CPA|the cost that leaves your margin
Scale line|0.8 × target, proof of a real winner
Kill lines|when an ad set is switched off
Test budget|planned spend per ad set
steps.say: Look at these six cards. Before any ad goes live, you write these six numbers on one page: the payout, break-even C P A, which means cost per acquisition, target C P A, the scale line, your kill lines, and your test budget. All six come from just two things, the payout and the margin you want to keep. The rest of this module uses them at every checkpoint. Get them right once, and you never have to argue with yourself later.

steps.p: Break-even CPA is the cost per conversion where you neither win nor lose. On a flat CPA deal it is simply the payout. Pay more than this per FTD and every FTD loses you money, however good the other numbers look.
steps.more: Example: the network pays $40 per qualified FTD. Break-even CPA is $40. If you pay $44 per FTD you lose $4 on each one. On RevShare or hybrid deals break-even depends on value over time, which is harder; for your first tests choose a flat CPA deal so this line is clear.
steps.say: First, break-even C P A. This is the cost per conversion where you neither win nor lose. On a flat C P A deal, it's simply the payout, just like the equation on screen. Here's an example. The network pays forty dollars per qualified F T D, a first-time deposit. Break-even is forty dollars. Pay forty four per F T D and you lose four dollars on each one. On RevShare or hybrid deals it's harder, so for your first tests, choose a flat C P A deal so this line is clear.

steps.p: Target CPA is the cost per conversion that leaves you the margin you chose. You multiply the payout by what is left after your margin. The margin covers tools, fees, rejected conversions and the noise in small tests, so do not set it at zero.
steps.say: Next, target C P A. This is the cost per conversion that leaves you the margin you chose. Follow the equation: payout, times one minus your margin, gives target C P A. Why keep a margin at all? Because it has to cover your tools, fees, rejected conversions and the noise you get in small tests. So never set the margin at zero. Paying exactly the payout leaves you no room for anything to go wrong.

steps.p: Example: payout $40 per FTD and you want to keep a 25% margin. One minus 25% is 75%. $40 × 75% = $30. Your target CPA is $30. This is the number every rule in this module is built on.
steps.more: Why 25%? It is a starting choice, not a law. A 10% margin leaves almost no room for rejected FTDs or a bad week. A 40% margin can make your target so low that almost nothing passes. Many beginners start between 20% and 30% and adjust once they have data. We use 25% for every Example in this module.
steps.say: Let's work one through. This is an example. The payout is forty dollars per F T D and you want to keep a twenty five percent margin. One minus twenty five percent is seventy five percent. Forty dollars times seventy five percent is thirty dollars. So your target C P A is thirty dollars. Why twenty five percent? It's a starting choice, not a law. Ten percent leaves almost no room for a bad week, and forty percent can make the target so low almost nothing passes. Many beginners start between twenty and thirty percent. We use twenty five for every example in this module.

steps.p: Try it. Enter the payout and the margin, then check your answer. The lead-to-deposit rate does not change the target CPA, only the cost per lead. Change the numbers afterwards to see how a thinner or fatter margin moves the line.

d.task: Payout $40 per FTD, margin 25%. What is your target CPA (max cost per FTD)?

steps.say: Now it's your turn. The payout is forty dollars per F T D and the margin is twenty five percent. What's your target C P A, the most you can pay per F T D? Enter the payout and the margin in the tool. One note: the lead-to-deposit rate doesn't change the target C P A, only the cost per lead. Pause and try it, then check your answer. Afterwards, change the numbers and watch how a thinner or fatter margin moves the line.

steps.p: The first kill line handles ad sets that bring nothing. When spend reaches 2 × target CPA and there are 0 network-confirmed conversions, you switch the ad set off. With a $30 target that line is $60.
steps.more: Why 2 × target and not 1 ×? One target CPA of spend gives an ad set roughly one fair chance at a conversion. Many decent ad sets miss that first one by luck. By 2 × target with nothing at all, the odds that it is a hidden winner are low enough that the money is better spent on a new ad set. Some guides use 2 × payout as a simple first threshold. Here we tighten it to 2 × target, which kills losers a little sooner.
steps.say: The first kill line handles ad sets that bring nothing at all. When spend reaches two times your target C P A and there are zero network-confirmed conversions, you switch the ad set off. With a thirty dollar target, that line is sixty dollars. Why two times and not one? One target C P A of spend gives roughly one fair chance at a conversion, and plenty of decent ad sets miss that first one by luck. Some guides use two times payout as a simple first threshold. Here we tighten it to two times target, which kills losers a little sooner.

steps.p: Example: all six numbers for one offer, worked out from a $40 payout and a 25% margin. Notice the CPA kill line. It is the lower of 1.5 × target and break-even, because you never want a rule that lets you keep paying more than the payout.
steps.say: Here's your full numbers sheet. This is an example, built from a forty dollar payout and a twenty five percent margin. Break-even is forty dollars, target is thirty, the scale line is twenty four, and the zero F T D kill is sixty. Now notice the C P A kill line. It's the lower of one point five times target and break-even, so here it's forty dollars. That's because you never want a rule that lets you keep paying more than the payout. And the test budget per ad set is sixty to ninety dollars.

steps.p: As a starting rule, plan 2 to 3 × target CPA of spend for each ad set. 2 × lets you apply the zero-conversion kill. 3 × lets you judge CPA on an ad set that does convert. Plan 3 × if you can afford it.
steps.more: Example: target $30. 2 × $30 = $60, 3 × $30 = $90. With three ad sets, the planned spend is $180 to $270. Add a 10% buffer for overspend and rounding: about $200 to $300. If that is more than you can afford to lose, test fewer ad sets, not smaller ones.
steps.say: How much should each ad set get? As a starting rule, plan two to three times target C P A per ad set. Two times lets you apply the zero conversion kill. Three times lets you actually judge C P A on an ad set that does convert, so plan three times if you can afford it. Example: with a thirty dollar target, that's sixty to ninety dollars. Three ad sets means one hundred eighty to two hundred seventy, plus a ten percent buffer, so about two to three hundred. If that's too much to lose, test fewer ad sets, not smaller ones.

steps.h: Lab: daily budget per ad set
steps.p: Turn the test budget into a daily budget. You want room for about 3 target CPAs in each ad set, spread over 6 days so that you see a full week of behaviour. Work it out, then check.

d.task: Room for 3 FTDs at a $30 target CPA over 6 days. What daily budget per ad set?

steps.say: Now turn that test budget into a daily budget. You want room for about three target C P As in each ad set, spread over six days, so you see a full week of behaviour. The task on screen gives you the numbers: room for three F T Ds at a thirty dollar target C P A, over six days. What daily budget per ad set does that give you? Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.p: Example, target $30. The daily budget decides how many days pass before you can apply each rule. Too small and the decisions take weeks. Too big and you reach the kill line on day one, before postbacks have time to arrive.
steps.say: This table shows why the daily budget matters. It's an example with a thirty dollar target. The daily budget decides how many days pass before you can apply each rule. Read across the rows. At ten dollars a day, it takes six days to reach the sixty dollar line. At thirty a day, just two. Too small, and decisions take weeks. Too big, and you hit the kill line on day one, before postbacks have had time to arrive.

steps.p: Example: the same $40 payout with three different margins. A bigger margin gives a lower target, so fewer ad sets pass, but the ones that pass are safer. Recalculate every line whenever you change the margin or the network changes the payout.
steps.say: Look at these bars. It's an example with the same forty dollar payout and three different margins. A ten percent margin gives a thirty six dollar target. Twenty five percent gives thirty. Forty percent gives twenty four. A bigger margin means a lower target, so fewer ad sets pass, but the ones that do are safer. And here's the habit to build: recalculate every line whenever you change your margin or the network changes the payout.

steps.h: Walkthrough: write the plan in a sheet
steps.p: Open a blank spreadsheet and make a plan tab before you open Ads Manager. Type the payout and margin, then let formulas fill the rest so a payout change updates every line. Screenshot it with the date. This tab is what you read at every checkpoint.

steps.p: Your numbers only mean something if the conversions are real and allowed. Trading, gambling and finance offers usually need platform authorization and must follow local law in each geo. Check both before you plan a budget.

takeaways: Target CPA = payout × (1 − margin). Break-even CPA on a flat deal = payout.
Zero-conversion kill line = 2 × target. CPA kill line = the lower of 1.5 × target and break-even.

lessons.title: The rule card: kill, hold, keep, scale
objectives: By the end you can apply exact kill, hold, keep and scale rules to an ad set's numbers.
By the end you can say which decisions are allowed at the 24, 48 and 72 hour checkpoints.
By the end you can explain why decisions use network-confirmed conversions.

steps.p: Every checkpoint ends with one of four decisions for each ad set. A rule card turns that into a lookup instead of a debate. Without it, a beginner usually keeps losers too long and starves winners, and both mistakes cost real money.

d.s: Starting rules; adapt to your vertical and data.

steps.say: Every checkpoint ends with one of four decisions for each ad set: kill, hold, keep or scale. A rule card turns that into a simple lookup instead of a debate with yourself. Without one, beginners usually keep losers too long and starve their winners, and both mistakes cost real money. As always, these are starting rules. Adapt them to your vertical and your data.

steps.p: These four words mean exact actions, not moods. Hold and Keep both leave the budget alone, but for different reasons: Hold means you cannot judge yet, Keep means you judged and it is working at target.
d: Kill|pause the ad set. Do not restart it
Hold|data too thin or CPA unclear. Change nothing
Keep|working at target. Leave the budget
Scale|clear winner. Add budget in a step
steps.say: Look at these four cards. These words mean exact actions, not moods. Kill means pause the ad set, and don't restart it. Hold means the data is too thin or the C P A, your cost per acquisition, is unclear, so you change nothing. Keep means it's working at target, so you leave the budget. Scale means a clear winner, so you add budget in a step. Notice Hold and Keep both leave the budget alone, but for different reasons. Hold means you can't judge yet. Keep means you judged, and it's working.

steps.p: Example with a $30 target, $40 break-even. Check the rows from the top and stop at the first one that is true. Starting rules; adapt them to your vertical and data. Count only network-confirmed conversions.

rows: Spend ≥ 3 × target and CPA above CPA kill line

steps.say: Here's the rule card itself. It's an example with a thirty dollar target and forty dollar break-even. Check the rows from the top and stop at the first one that's true. Kill with zero conversions at sixty dollars spent. Kill when spend is ninety or more and C P A is over forty. Scale with three or more F T Ds, first-time deposits, at a C P A of twenty four or less. Keep with three or more at twenty four to thirty. Anything else is Hold. Count only network-confirmed conversions, and adapt these starting rules to your data.

steps.h: The rule card as a decision tree
steps.p: The same card as a path. Start at the checkpoint and answer each question with yes or no. The first yes gives your decision. If you reach the end with no yes, the answer is Hold, and you change nothing until the next checkpoint.
steps.say: This is the same card drawn as a path. Start at the checkpoint on the left and answer each question, yes or no. Zero F T Ds with spend at two times target? Kill. Spend at three times with C P A over the kill line? Kill. Three plus F T Ds with C P A at zero point eight times target or less? Scale by twenty percent. Three plus at or under target? Keep. If you reach the end with no yes at all, the answer is Hold, and you change nothing until the next checkpoint.

steps.h: Why the CPA kill line uses break-even
steps.p: The free Kill-or-scale tool kills on CPA above 1.5 × target. With a 25% margin, 1.5 × target is above your payout, so you would keep paying more than you earn. Our card uses the lower of the two.
steps.more: When is 1.5 × target the lower one? Only when your margin is above about 33%. Example: payout $60, margin 40%, target $36. 1.5 × $36 = $54, below the $60 break-even, so $54 is the kill line. Work this out once per offer and write the result on your plan tab.

d.text: Example: target $30. 1.5 × $30 = $45. Payout $40. The CPA kill line is $40, the lower one.

steps.say: Here's why our C P A kill line uses break-even. The free Kill-or-scale tool kills on C P A above one point five times target. But with a twenty five percent margin, one point five times target is above your payout, so you'd keep paying more than you earn. Look at the example on screen: target thirty, so one point five times is forty five, but the payout is forty, so the kill line is forty, the lower one. One point five times target is only lower when your margin is above about thirty three percent. Work it out once per offer and write it on your plan tab.

steps.h: What you may decide, and when
steps.p: Timing matters as much as the numbers. Early hours show whether things work, not whether they pay. These are starting rules for an FTD offer with postbacks that usually arrive the same day. Slow postbacks need the rules in the next lesson.

rows: All four, scale steps ≥ 48 h apart

steps.say: Timing matters as much as the numbers. Early hours show whether things work, not whether they pay. In the first six hours, you check the ad is approved, spending and the link works, and you only fix things. At twenty four hours you look at C T R, click-through rate, C P C, cost per click, page views and sign-ups, and the only kill allowed is the zero F T D kill. At forty eight hours, kill rules apply. At seventy two, kill, keep and scale. After that, all four, with scale steps at least forty eight hours apart. This assumes postbacks usually arrive the same day. Slow postbacks need the next lesson.

steps.h: Confirmed by the network, not the platform
steps.p: Ads Manager reports what its pixel or conversions API saw. The network reports what it will pay for. They often differ: duplicate events, deposits under the minimum, rejected or held FTDs. Your rule card uses the network number, because that is the money.

d.b: Judge with what you get paid for
d.s: The platform number guides delivery, not decisions

steps.say: This is a crucial point. Ads Manager reports what its pixel or conversions A P I saw. The network reports what it will actually pay for. They often differ, because of duplicate events, deposits under the minimum, and rejected or held F T Ds. Your rule card uses the network number, because that's the money. The platform number guides delivery. It doesn't make your decisions.

steps.p: Example: the same ad set on the same day. Using the platform number, CPA looks like $20 and you would scale. Using the network number, CPA is $40, which is break-even, so the card says Hold at best. One wrong column can double your spend on a loser.
steps.say: Compare the two columns. It's an example: the same ad set on the same day, eighty dollars spent. The platform says four purchases, a C P A of twenty dollars, which looks like Scale. The network confirms only two qualified F T Ds, so the C P A is forty dollars. That's break-even, so the card says Hold at best, close to kill. Reading the wrong column could double your spend on a loser.

Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.p: One more. The CPA is above target, but how much has it spent compared with 3 × target? In the tool, Keep shows as Hold, because the action is the same: no budget change.

The C P A is above target, but ask yourself, how much has it spent compared with three times target? One note on the tool: Keep shows up as Hold, because the action is the same, no budget change. Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.h: How long a Hold can last
steps.p: Hold is not forever. An ad set stuck above target eats budget that a new ad set could use. These limits stop a Hold from turning into a slow leak. Starting rules; adapt to your vertical and data.
steps.more: Example: target $30, kill line $40. An ad set has spent $96 with 3 FTDs, CPA $32. It is above target but under the kill line, so Hold. Two days later it has spent $126 with 4 FTDs, CPA $31.50. Still above target after 2 more checkpoints, so kill it and move the money to a new angle.
d: Re-check at the next daily checkpoint
Above target after 2 more checkpoints: kill
Spend reaches 5 × target, CPA still above target: kill
To try a new creative, launch it as a new ad set
steps.say: Hold isn't forever. An ad set stuck above target eats budget a new ad set could use. So here are the limits. Change nothing while in Hold. Re-check at the next daily checkpoint. If it's still above target after two more checkpoints, kill it. If spend reaches five times target and C P A is still above target, kill it. And to try a new creative, launch it as a new ad set. Example: an ad set spent ninety six dollars for three F T Ds, thirty two each, so Hold. Two days later it's at thirty one fifty. Still above target, so kill it and move the money to a new angle.

steps.p: These are the ways beginners break their own card. Each one feels reasonable in the moment, which is why the card has to be written before launch and read at every checkpoint.

b.title: Fixes
items: Launch a new ad set instead

steps.say: These are the ways beginners break their own card. Killing on C T R at six hours. Scaling on one cheap F T D. Using platform conversions. Reviving a killed ad set. Raising budget on a Hold. And on the right, the fixes: no C P A decisions before forty eight hours, scaling needs three or more F T Ds, use network-confirmed only, launch a new ad set instead of reviving, and Hold means no change. Each mistake feels reasonable in the moment, which is why the card is written before launch.

lessons.say_intro: In this lesson you'll build your rule card, the one page that turns every checkpoint into kill, hold, keep or scale. You'll also learn when each decision is allowed and why we only trust network-confirmed conversions.

lessons.title: Rules when data is thin or late
objectives: By the end you can find your network's postback delay and use only matured spend for CPA decisions.
By the end you can use a proxy metric to spot a weak ad set early without scaling on it.
By the end you can size a small budget so the rule card still works.

steps.h: Late data kills good ad sets
steps.p: If FTDs reach your network hours after the spend, today's numbers always look worse than they are. Judge too early and you kill ad sets that were working. Panic the other way and you feed losers. Both cost money, so late data needs its own rules.

d.s: Starting rules; adapt to your vertical and data.

steps.say: If first-time deposits, or F T Ds, reach your network hours after the spend, today's numbers will always look worse than they really are. Judge too early, and you kill ad sets that were actually working. Panic the other way, and you feed losers. Both cost money. So late data needs its own rules. Today's spend often means tomorrow's F T Ds. These are starting rules, so adapt them to your vertical and data.

steps.p: Four things push conversions after the spend that caused them. You cannot remove them, so you measure them and plan around them. Ask your network manager about each one before your first test.
d: Deposit delay|people sign up today, deposit days later
Postback delay|the network sends the event minutes to hours later
Holds and review|FTDs sit as pending before approval
Time zones|the ad account day and network day differ
steps.say: Look at these four cards. Four things push conversions later than the spend that caused them. Deposit delay: people sign up today but deposit days later. Postback delay: the network sends the event minutes to hours later. Holds and review: F T Ds sit as pending before approval. And time zones: the ad account day and the network day differ. You can't remove these, so you measure them and plan around them. Ask your network manager about each one before your first test.

steps.h: One day's spend, counted over time
steps.p: Example: one ad set spent $45 on Monday. Watch how the confirmed counts for that same day keep rising for days. A CPA read on Monday night would be wrong, and a kill decision based on it would be wrong too.
steps.say: Watch this chart. It's an example: one ad set spent forty five dollars on Monday. The top line shows sign-ups from that Monday, and the lower line shows F T Ds from that same Monday. Notice how both keep rising for days. F T Ds go from zero at the start to three by day seven. A C P A, or cost per acquisition, read on Monday night would be wrong, and a kill decision based on it would be wrong too.

steps.p: Do this once per offer after your first few conversions. You compare the click time with the conversion time in the network's report. The typical gap is your lag. Write it on your plan tab.

steps.title: Open the conversions report
steps.text: In the network dashboard, open the conversion or FTD report and add columns for click time and conversion time. Names vary by network.

steps.title: Work out each gap
steps.text: Subtract click time from FTD time for each row. Example: 9 h 28 min, 11 h 35 min, 13 h 46 min.

blocks.value: Most FTDs arrive within about 12 hours (Example).

steps.title: Write the lag on your plan
steps.text: Round up to a safe number and use it at every checkpoint. Re-check after 20 or so FTDs.

steps.say: Here's how to measure your postback delay. Do this once per offer after your first few conversions. Tap Next to follow each step. First, open the conversions report in your network dashboard and add columns for click time and conversion time. Names vary by network. Second, work out each gap by subtracting click time from F T D time. In the example, the gaps are about nine and a half, eleven and a half, and nearly fourteen hours, so most arrive within about twelve. Third, round up to a safe number, write the lag on your plan, and re-check after twenty or so F T Ds.

steps.p: Matured spend is spend old enough that its conversions have had time to arrive. If your lag is 12 hours, matured spend is everything spent more than 12 hours ago. Kill lines and CPA are checked against matured spend only.

d.b: Judge only spend that has had time to convert
d.s: Matured spend = spend older than your lag

steps.say: Now the key rule. Matured spend is spend that's old enough for its conversions to have had time to arrive. If your lag is twelve hours, matured spend is everything you spent more than twelve hours ago. From now on, your kill lines and your C P A are checked against matured spend only. Judge only the spend that's had time to convert.

steps.p: Example: target $30, zero-FTD kill line $60, lag 12 hours, $30 a day. At 48 hours the ad set shows $60 spent and 0 FTDs. It looks like a kill. But only $45 of that spend is matured, so the kill waits until the 60-hour check.
steps.say: Let's see it in action. This is an example: target thirty dollars, zero F T D kill line sixty, lag twelve hours, thirty dollars a day. At forty eight hours, the ad set shows sixty dollars spent and zero F T Ds. That looks like a kill. But read the second row. Only forty five dollars of that spend is matured. So the decision at forty eight hours is Hold. If it's still at zero by the sixty hour check, the matured spend reaches sixty, and then it's a kill.

steps.p: Use matured spend as the spend figure. Then apply the rule card from the top. A zero is not a kill until the matured spend reaches 2 × target.

d.task: Target $30. Matured spend $45 over 3 days, 0 network-confirmed FTDs. Kill, hold or scale?

steps.say: Your turn. Target thirty dollars. Matured spend is forty five dollars over three days, with zero network-confirmed F T Ds. Is it kill, hold or scale? Use the matured spend as your spend figure, then apply the rule card from the top. Remember, a zero isn't a kill until matured spend reaches two times target. Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.h: Proxy metric: target cost per sign-up
steps.p: When FTDs are slow, an earlier step can warn you. Multiply your target CPA by the sign-up-to-FTD rate the network or your past data gives you. That is the most you should pay per sign-up.
steps.more: Example: target $30 and about 20% of sign-ups deposit (rough guide from your network; varies by geo and vertical). $30 × 20% = $6 per sign-up. Warning rule: if cost per sign-up is above 2 × that ($12) once matured spend reaches 1 × target ($30), the ad set is unlikely to hit target. You may kill early or plan a replacement. A proxy can trigger an early kill. It can never trigger a scale: only confirmed FTDs do that.
steps.say: When F T Ds are slow, an earlier step in the funnel can warn you. Follow the equation: target C P A times your sign-up to F T D rate gives your target cost per sign-up. Example: target thirty dollars and about twenty percent of sign-ups deposit. That's a rough guide, and it varies by geo and vertical. So the target is six dollars per sign-up. If cost per sign-up is above twice that, twelve dollars, once matured spend reaches thirty, you may kill early. But here's the rule: a proxy can trigger an early kill. It can never trigger a scale. Only confirmed F T Ds do that.

steps.p: Example: target cost per sign-up $6, warning line $12. An ad set has $30 of matured spend and 2 sign-ups, so $15 per sign-up. That is above $12. You may kill it now rather than wait for $60, or keep it to the zero-FTD line if you have no replacement ready.

d.text: $30 ÷ 2 sign-ups = $15. Above the $12 warning line. Early kill allowed, scale never on a proxy.

steps.say: Here's that early warning in action. It's an example. Target cost per sign-up is six dollars, so the warning line is twelve. An ad set has thirty dollars of matured spend and two sign-ups. Thirty divided by two is fifteen dollars per sign-up, which is above twelve. You may kill it now rather than wait for sixty. Or, if you have no replacement ready, keep it running to the zero F T D line. Early kill is allowed. Scale on a proxy, never.

steps.p: Example: target $30, so the zero-FTD kill line is $60. At $5 a day per ad set, it takes 12 days to reach it. Starting rule: give each ad set at least half your target CPA per day, so the kill line arrives within about 4 days.

d.label: to reach a $60 kill line at $5 a day

steps.say: Look at that big number: twelve days. Here's the example. Target thirty dollars, so the zero F T D kill line is sixty. At five dollars a day per ad set, it takes twelve days to reach it. That's far too slow. So here's a starting rule: give each ad set at least half your target C P A per day, so the kill line arrives within about four days.

steps.p: Example: $45 a day total, target $30. Split across 9 ad sets, each needs 12 days to reach the kill line. Split across 3, each gets there in 4 days. If money is tight, cut the number of ad sets, not the budget per ad set.
steps.say: These bars show the same money split different ways. It's an example: forty five dollars a day total, with a thirty dollar target. Split across nine ad sets at five dollars, each needs twelve days to reach the kill line. Five ad sets at nine dollars, about six point seven days. Three ad sets at fifteen dollars, just four days. So if money is tight, cut the number of ad sets, not the budget per ad set.

steps.h: The learning phase: what we know
steps.p: At the time of writing, Meta describes a learning phase that an ad set leaves after roughly 50 optimisation events in about a week. We are not certain this threshold is current; check Meta's Help Center. Small beginner ad sets often never leave it. Judge with your rule card, not the learning label.

steps.h: What not to do with thin data
steps.p: Thin data tempts you into action. Almost every action here makes the data thinner or noisier. When in doubt between doing something and waiting for the next checkpoint, wait, unless something is broken.

a.title: Do not
items: Kill at 6 hours on zero FTDs
Raise budget to get data faster
Edit the ad set every day
Switch it off and on to reset it

b.title: Do instead
items: Launch a new ad set for a new idea

steps.say: Thin data tempts you into action, and almost every action makes the data thinner or noisier. On the left, what not to do: kill at six hours on zero F T Ds, count unmatured spend in C P A, raise budget to get data faster, edit the ad set every day, or switch it off and on to reset it. On the right, what to do instead: fix only broken things early, use matured spend, keep the planned budget, wait for the next checkpoint, and launch a new ad set for a new idea. When in doubt, wait, unless something's broken.

steps.p: Some buyers send extra or invented conversion events to the ad platform to push the ad set out of learning. That is sending false data and breaks platform rules. Pending FTDs that the network later rejects for fraud or self-deposits can also cost you the account.

d.text: Send only real events. Never deposit yourself or pay people to deposit to make numbers move.

lessons.title: Scaling rules and when to stop
objectives: By the end you can scale a winning ad set in exact +20% steps with the right waiting time.
By the end you can choose between raising budget, duplicating and scaling sideways.
By the end you can apply stop-scaling rules that protect profit, not just volume.

steps.p: Scaling is where profit grows, and where losses grow fastest. A $15 ad set that slips above break-even loses a few dollars. The same ad set at $60 a day loses four times as much, every day. So scaling has entry rules, step rules and stop rules.

d.s: Starting rules; adapt to your vertical and data.

steps.say: Scaling is where profit grows, and it's also where losses grow fastest. A fifteen dollar ad set that slips above break-even loses a few dollars. The same ad set at sixty dollars a day loses four times as much, every single day. So scaling has entry rules, step rules and stop rules. Earn each step with data. These are starting rules, so adapt them to your vertical and data.

steps.p: An ad set may get its first budget step only when all three are true: at least 3 network-confirmed conversions, CPA at or under 0.8 × target, and at least 72 hours running. This is the Scale row of the rule card.
steps.say: Here's the entry rule. An ad set can get its first budget step only when all three parts of this equation are true. At least three network-confirmed F T Ds, first-time deposits. A C P A, cost per acquisition, at or under zero point eight times target. And at least seventy two hours running. When all three line up, you step up twenty percent. This is simply the Scale row of your rule card.

steps.p: Example: start at $15 a day, target $30. Each step adds 20% to the current budget. At least 48 hours pass between steps, and each step has to be earned again. The days shown are the earliest possible, not a promise.
steps.say: Look at this step plan. It's an example: start at fifteen dollars a day with a thirty dollar target. Each step adds twenty percent to the current budget. Fifteen goes to eighteen, then twenty one sixty, then twenty five ninety two, then thirty one ten. At least forty eight hours pass between steps, and each step has to be earned again. The days in the right column are the earliest possible, not a promise.

steps.h: The rule for every next step
steps.p: After a step, the new budget has to prove itself. Look at the numbers since the last step, not the lifetime total, because the lifetime number hides a slipping CPA. Starting rules; adapt to your vertical and data.
steps.more: Example: target $30, scale line $24. After stepping to $18, two days pass: $36 spent, 2 FTDs since the step, $18 CPA. Lifetime: $96 for 5 FTDs, $19.20. Both are under $24, so step again to $21.60. If those two days had brought 1 FTD, $36 CPA since the step, you would not step. You would Keep at $18 and check again tomorrow.
d: At least 48 hours since the last step
At least 2 network FTDs since the step
Any miss: no step, Keep or Hold
steps.say: After a step, the new budget has to prove itself. Here are the rules for every next step: at least forty eight hours since the last step, at least two network F T Ds since the step, C P A since the step at zero point eight times target or less, and lifetime C P A still under that line too. Any miss means no step, just Keep or Hold. Why look since the step? Because the lifetime number hides a slipping C P A. Example: after stepping to eighteen, two days bring two F T Ds for thirty six dollars, eighteen each, so you step again. If they'd brought only one, you'd Keep at eighteen.

steps.p: These are lifetime numbers for an ad set that has run 6 days. Apply the scale row. Then imagine the same spend with 3 FTDs and see how the answer changes.

Is it kill, hold or scale? Apply the scale row of your card. Pause and try it, then check your answer. Afterwards, imagine the same spend with only three F T Ds and see how the answer changes.

steps.p: Example: daily budget and CPA since the last step for one ad set. Budget rises in steps. CPA wobbles but stays under the $24 scale line, so each step is earned. The moment the CPA line crosses $24, steps stop.
steps.say: Watch the two lines on this chart. It's an example for one ad set. The daily budget rises in steps, from fifteen to eighteen to twenty one sixty. The other line is C P A since the last step. It wobbles, but it stays under the twenty four dollar scale line, so each step is earned. The moment the C P A line crosses twenty four, the steps stop.

steps.p: Example, target $30, break-even $40. These rules decide when to stop raising, step back or hand the ad set back to the rule card. Write them under your rule card. Starting rules; adapt to your vertical and data.

rows: CPA since step above $24 for 48 h
CPA since step above $30 for 48 h
Back to the last budget that worked
Back one step now; rule card at next check
Stop raising; budget to fit the cap
CTR down 30%+ from its best, frequency rising

steps.say: These are the stop-scaling rules. It's an example with a thirty dollar target and forty dollar break-even. If C P A since the step is above twenty four for forty eight hours, no more steps, just Keep. Above thirty for forty eight hours, go back to the last budget that worked. Above forty, step back one now, then use the rule card at the next check. If the network cap is nearly full, stop raising. And if C T R, your click-through rate, drops thirty percent or more from its best while frequency rises, add new creatives before any step. Write these under your rule card.

steps.p: Raising the budget is only one way. Once a winner has passed two steps, you can also copy it or take its idea sideways. Each way has its own risk, so use them in this order.
d: Vertical|raise the winner's budget in +20% steps
Duplicate|copy the winner at its start budget
Horizontal|same creative, new angle, placement or geo
Feed it|add new ads to the winning ad set's idea
steps.say: Raising the budget is only one way to scale. Look at these four cards. Vertical: raise the winner's budget in plus twenty percent steps. Duplicate: copy the winner at its start budget. Horizontal: the same creative, but a new angle, placement or geo. And feed it: add new ads to the winning ad set's idea. Each has its own risk, so use them in this order, and only once a winner has passed two steps for the copying and sideways moves.

steps.p: A duplicate is a new ad set. It starts at zero data and goes through the full rule card from day one. Most failed duplicates fail because buyers give them the winner's raised budget and judge them on the winner's history.
d: Only after the original passed 2 steps
Start at the original start budget, not the raised one
Full rule card from zero, own checkpoints
At most 2 duplicates per winner at once
If a duplicate fails, kill it, not the original
steps.say: A duplicate is a new ad set. It starts at zero data and goes through the full rule card from day one. Here are the rules. Only duplicate after the original has passed two steps. Start at the original start budget, not the raised one. Run the full rule card from zero with its own checkpoints. No more than two duplicates per winner at once. And if a duplicate fails, kill the duplicate, not the original. Most failed duplicates fail because buyers give them the winner's raised budget and judge them on the winner's history.

steps.h: More spend is not more profit
steps.p: Example, $40 payout. Profit per day = FTDs per day × $40 − spend. Doubling to $30 a day raises CPA a little and profit a little. Doubling again to $60 pushes CPA to $36 and profit falls. The aim is the most profit, not the biggest budget.
steps.more: Working: $15 ÷ $20 = 0.75 FTDs a day × $40 = $30 revenue − $15 = $15 profit. $30 ÷ $26 = 1.154 FTDs × $40 = $46.15 − $30 = $16.15. $60 ÷ $36 = 1.667 FTDs × $40 = $66.67 − $60 = $6.67. This is why the stop rules look at CPA since the step, not just whether the ad set is still profitable.
steps.say: More spend isn't always more profit. It's an example with a forty dollar payout. At fifteen dollars a day and a twenty dollar C P A, profit is fifteen dollars a day. Doubling to thirty a day pushes C P A to twenty six, and profit rises only a little, to about sixteen fifteen. Doubling again to sixty pushes C P A to thirty six, and profit falls to about six sixty seven. Look at how short that last bar is. The aim is the most profit, not the biggest budget. That's why the stop rules look at C P A since the step.

steps.h: Same time, same steps, every day

objectives: By the end you can set a maximum loss per test, per day and per week from your bankroll.

steps.h: Ad set rules protect ad sets. Caps protect you.
steps.p: The rule card decides about one ad set at a time. It cannot see that you have lost three tests in a row or that a budget typo spent $300 overnight. Bankroll caps are the rules above the card: how much you can lose on a test, in a day and in a week.

steps.say: The rule card decides about one ad set at a time. But it can't see that you've lost three tests in a row, or that a budget typo spent three hundred dollars overnight. That's what bankroll caps are for. They're the rules above the card: how much you can lose on a test, in a day and in a week. Ad set rules protect ad sets. Caps protect you. These are starting rules, so adapt them to your situation.

steps.p: These four numbers come from your bankroll, the money set aside only for ads and tools. The Operator habits module covers how to build that bankroll. Here we turn it into hard stop lines that work alongside the rule card.
d: Per test|the most one test may lose

steps.say: Look at these four cards. Per test, the most one test may lose. Per day, the most all your campaigns may lose in a day. Per week, the most all your tests may lose in a week. And the bankroll floor, the level where all new tests stop. They all come from your bankroll, the money set aside only for ads and tools. The Operator habits module covers how to build that bankroll. Here, we turn it into hard stop lines.

steps.p: Example. The percentages are starting rules for beginners; adapt them to your situation. Loss means spend minus network-confirmed revenue, counted on matured spend. The weekly cap is lower than two full tests so one bad week cannot take a big bite.
steps.say: Here are example caps from a two thousand dollar bankroll. The percentages are starting rules for beginners. Per test, ten to twenty percent of bankroll, and we use fifteen, so three hundred dollars. Per day, five percent, one hundred dollars. Per week, twenty five percent, five hundred dollars. And the floor, half the starting bankroll, one thousand dollars. Loss means spend minus network-confirmed revenue, counted on matured spend. Notice the weekly cap is lower than two full tests, so one bad week can't take a big bite.

steps.h: Does the test fit its cap?
steps.p: Before launch, check that the planned test budget plus a 10% buffer is at or under the per-test cap. If it is over, cut ad sets, not the budget per ad set, as you learned in lessons 1 and 3.
steps.more: Example: 3 ad sets × 3 × $30 target = $270. Plus 10% = $297. That is under the $300 cap, so the plan fits. With 4 ad sets the plan would be $360 + $36 = $396, over the cap, so you would drop one ad set or plan 2 × target ($60) each: 4 × $60 = $240 + $24 = $264.
steps.say: Before launch, check the test fits its cap. Follow the equation: test budget, plus a ten percent buffer, must be at or under the per-test cap. Example: three ad sets times three times a thirty dollar target is two hundred seventy, plus ten percent is two hundred ninety seven. That's under three hundred, so it fits. With four ad sets you'd be at three hundred ninety six, over the cap. So drop one ad set, or plan two times target each, which gives two hundred sixty four. Cut ad sets, not the budget per ad set.

steps.h: When to stop the whole test
steps.p: Any one of these ends the test, even if one ad set looks promising. Stopping is not failing; it is keeping money for a better test. Write these under your rule card. Starting rules; adapt to your vertical and data.

rows: Net loss reaches the per-test cap
All ad sets killed, no new creative ready
3 rounds, no ad set reached Keep
Stop; change offer, geo or angle
Payout cut, cap full or offer paused
Same ad rejected twice for policy

steps.say: Any one of these six triggers ends the whole test, even if one ad set looks promising. Net loss reaches the per-test cap. All ad sets killed and no new creative ready. Three rounds with no ad set reaching Keep. Tracking or postbacks broken. Payout cut, cap full or offer paused. And the same ad rejected twice for policy. Read the action next to each one. Stopping isn't failing. It's keeping money for a better test. Write these under your rule card.

steps.p: If one day's net loss passes the daily cap, something is usually wrong rather than unlucky: a budget typed as $150 instead of $15, a duplicated campaign, a broken link. Pause everything and find the cause before the next day starts.

steps.say: The daily cap is great at catching errors. If one day's net loss passes it, something is usually wrong rather than unlucky. A budget typed as one hundred fifty instead of fifteen. A duplicated campaign. A broken link. Look at the example: the daily cap is one hundred dollars and Wednesday's loss is one hundred ten. So you pause everything, check budgets, links and postbacks, and restart only after you've found the cause.

steps.h: A week against the weekly cap
steps.p: Example: cumulative loss across all tests over one week, against a $500 weekly cap. Wednesday passes the daily cap, so everything pauses Thursday while the error is found. The week ends at $350, under the cap.

On Wednesday, the loss jumps by one hundred ten, past the daily cap, so everything pauses on Thursday while the error is found. That's why the line is flat there. The week ends at three hundred fifty dollars, under the cap.

steps.p: If your bankroll falls to half its starting size, stop launching new tests for at least a week. Review every note, then change one big thing: offer, geo, source or vertical. Running the same kind of test with less money rarely ends differently.

steps.say: Caps fail in predictable ways, mostly after a loss. Raising the cap mid-test. Saying one more day after hitting the cap. Restarting killed ad sets to win the money back. Borrowing to refill the bankroll. And the fixes: change caps only between tests, cap reached means stop today, run a new test with a new question, and wait, review, and rebuild from income. A cap you move in the middle of a test isn't a cap. Decide caps on a calm day, in writing.

steps.p: When an account hits a limit, gets restricted or is banned, the honest move is to stop, read the reason and appeal through official channels. Never open new accounts, use someone else's card or rent accounts to keep spending.

exam.q: Payout $50, margin 30%. An ad set has spent $72 with 0 network-confirmed FTDs after 3 days. What do you do?

exam.q: Target $30, break-even $40. Spent $95, 2 FTDs after 5 days. What does the rule card say?
options: Kill: spend is over 3 × target and CPA $47.50 is above the $40 kill line
exam.why: $95 ≥ $90 and $95 ÷ 2 = $47.50, above the lower kill line of $40.

exam.q: Target $25. At 72 hours: $57 spent, 3 FTDs. What do you do?
Ads Manager shows 6 conversions on $90; the network approved 2. Target $30, break-even $40. What is your decision?
options: Kill: network CPA $45 is above the $40 kill line at 3 × target spend
exam.why: Decisions use the network count: $90 ÷ 2 = $45, above $40, with spend at 3 × target.

exam.q: Postback lag 24 hours, $20 a day, target $30. At 72 hours: $60 spent, 0 FTDs. What do you do?
options: Hold: matured spend is $40, under the $60 line
exam.why: Only spend older than 24 hours counts: $40. The zero-FTD kill waits until matured spend reaches $60.

options: Early kill, cost per sign-up is too high
On track: $7.50 per sign-up is under the $12 warning line; Hold
exam.why: Target per sign-up = $30 × 20% = $6, warning line $12. $30 ÷ 4 = $7.50 is under it, and spend is under the $60 kill line.

exam.q: You stepped an ad set from $20 to $24 two days ago. Since then: $48 spent, 1 FTD. Target $30. What now?

exam.why: CPA since the step above target for 48 hours means back to the last budget that worked.

options: No: $480 + 10% = $528 is over $450; cut to 3 ad sets
Yes, caps do not include buffer
No, cut each ad set to $20

exam.q: Daily cap $100. Overnight an ad set spent $160 because the budget was typed as $160 instead of $16. What is the right order?
options: Pause all, fix the budget, then restart with the same rules
Leave it, the rule card will catch it
exam.why: Passing the daily cap signals an error. Pause, fix the cause, then continue under the same rules.

exam.q: Target $30. Ad set has 12 FTDs at a $17 CPA. A beginner asks whether to raise budget by 50%. Best answer?
